caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: DANDI:001453
attempts.paper_title: Neural circuits underlying divergent visuomotor strategies of zebrafish and Danionella cerebrum
attempts.entry_title: Optomotor swimming of zebrafish and Danionella cerebrum (Fouke et al. 2025)
attempts.description: Tests the freely swimming findings of Fouke, He, Loring and Naumann (2025) on dandiset 001453, which holds the tracking data of 25 zebrafish and 12 Danionella cerebrum larvae during the optomotor protocol. It compares swimming speed, turning and angular acceleration between species and stimuli, the response to monocular stimuli, and how steady the swimming is. The imaging and head-fixed tail tracking of the paper's Figures 2 to 4 are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Fouke et al. (2025) from dandiset 001453

outcomes.statement: The dandiset's stimulus codes can be linked to the stimuli the paper names, using the paper's analysis code and the protocol file of its stimulus software, and the values computed through that link agree with those the paper's code printed.
outcomes.source: Data and Code Availability; the paper's Fig1-S1.ipynb at GitLab commit 33a5c29
outcomes.notes: Codes are matched by their integer value. All 21 codes are in the dandiset, including every code the analysis uses. Through the link, 17 of 18 species and stimulus speed medians are within 10% of the values printed by Fig1-S1.ipynb (DC static is 10.52 against 11.9 mm/s), and the angular velocities differ from the printed ones by a median of 0.02 deg/s. The fish counts (25 ZF, 12 DC) match the code's lists; fish cannot be matched one by one, as no identifier links the dandiset's subjects to the code's folders. The static window is the code's (first 35 s of the code-20 block, measured from 3 s), and no fish median is exactly 0, so the code's exclusion of zero medians changes nothing. On codes 9 and 11 the ZF medians are 0.02 and 1.59 deg/s. Over 3 to 35 s DC turn more to the right for code 11 than for code 9 (median difference 5.82 deg/s, 10 of 12 fish, Wilcoxon p = 0.0093), and ZF go the same way without significance (1.66 deg/s, 16 of 25 fish, p = 0.141). If fish turn with lateral motion as they do with medial motion, code 11 is lateral right, as the protocol file has it; the data do not show that they do, so the assignment is not settled.
deviations: The code's filter on a `vel` column is not applied to DC trials, as the DC files have no such series; this is the remaining difference that may explain the one DC static value outside 10%.
The timing of the DC stimulus labels could not be confirmed from the turning response (the contrast is 4.6 deg/s with true labels and 0.1 with shifted ones); the DC labels are taken as they are.

outcomes.statement: Danionella cerebrum (DC) swim at a higher median velocity than zebrafish (ZF) across the visual stimuli.
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: DC show a significantly higher median velocity across all stimuli than ZF
outcomes.notes: Over all 21 codes, the median over fish and code values is 94.0 pixels/s for DC and 55.2 for ZF; species effect F = 78.4, p = 6.3e-18. The ANOVA treats each fish and code value as independent; with one value per fish, DC 87.4 against ZF 52.9 pixels/s, Mann-Whitney p = 0.02. With positions resampled to 30 Hz, 95.2 against 53.8 (p = 1.3e-08). DC are faster within each frame-rate group.
deviations: Tested over all stimulus codes without their names; the paper's figure uses nine whole-field stimuli.
The comparison assumes one spatial scale for all rigs, which the files do not state.

outcomes.statement: Across the whole-field stimuli DC have a higher median velocity than ZF (9.8 against 6.4 mm/s), with a significant main effect of species in a two-way ANOVA.
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: In contrast, DC show a significantly higher median velocity across all stimuli than ZF (DC = 9.8 mm/s, ZF = 6.4 mm/s
outcomes.notes: All four readings put both values within tolerance; (a) median of stimulus medians DC 10.02 and ZF 6.39 mm/s, (b) median of fish and stimulus values 9.87 and 6.41 (given as measured), (c) median of fish medians 9.36 and 6.33, (d) median of trials 9.88 and 6.28. Species effect F = 20.8, p = 7.5e-06. With 30 Hz positions DC 9.43 to 10.15 and ZF 6.07 to 6.30 (p = 0.0011). Without the trial rejection (4487 trials in place of 4458) readings (a) to (c) are unchanged and (d) gives DC 9.85 and ZF 6.30 (p = 6.7e-06).
deviations: The paper does not say how the overall median is taken; four readings are shown, and all match.
Speeds rely on the code's scale of 10 pixels per mm, which the dandiset does not state.

outcomes.statement: ZF modulate their velocity with the direction of motion; forward motion increases their median velocity (static 5.0 mm/s, forward 8.8 mm/s).
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: ZF strongly modulate their velocity depending on the motion direction, e.g., with forward motion increasing velocity (static = 5.0 mm/s, forward = 8.8 mm/s)
outcomes.notes: ZF static 4.84 mm/s over 18 fish and forward 8.78 mm/s over 25 fish. Of 18 fish with both, 14 are faster to forward motion (median difference 3.67 mm/s, Wilcoxon p = 0.0077). The static value is 8.31 mm/s in the 5 fish from 167 to 171 Hz files and 4.50 in the 13 from 32 to 35 Hz files. Static is the start of the blank block after all motion trials (4 hours in the protocol, 0.2 to 787.3 min in the files), one period per fish, and 7 ZF have none.

outcomes.statement: DC lack the direction-dependent velocity modulation seen in ZF.
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1; Figure 1D legend
outcomes.quote: In contrast, DC show a significantly higher median velocity across all stimuli than ZF ... and lacks direction-dependent velocity modulation
outcomes.notes: By the paper's test (Tukey's HSD over the 18 species and stimulus groups) 3 of 36 DC pairs differ, all static against a motion direction (backward left, backward right, forward left; adjusted p 0.030 to 0.049). The DC static values come from 9 fish and include one at 106.5 mm/s and two near 0. Among the eight directions no DC pair differs (smallest adjusted p 0.999), DC per-stimulus medians span 8.81 to 10.52 mm/s (ratio 1.19, ZF 2.03), and a one-way ANOVA across the nine DC stimuli gives p = 0.479 (ZF p = 0.00082). With values above 100 mm/s left out, no DC pair differs. The same Tukey test finds no ZF pair over the 18 groups (smallest p 0.835). The printed output of Fig1-S1.ipynb finds the same three DC pairs significant (adjusted p 0.0236, 0.0373 and 0.0397), so the paper's own test disagrees with the claim and this result matches the paper's computation. The DC-sub-2 static value of 106.5 mm/s is one trial measured over a 14.6 s motion phase in a 100 mm dish, likely a tracking artefact. It passes the code's speed check because the check covers 0 to 35 s (21.9 mm/s from the stored `dist`, 92.5 from positions); computing the check from positions, or leaving out zero medians as the code does, gives the same 3 pairs. The outcome is a property of the paper's test on this data, not evidence that DC modulate their speed with stimulus direction.
deviations: The DC static block is the code's window, but the code's filter on DC `vel` cannot be applied (DC static 10.52 against the code's printed 11.9 mm/s).

outcomes.statement: DC swim at a significantly higher velocity than ZF for oblique stimuli.
outcomes.source: Figure 1D legend
outcomes.quote: DC swims at a statistically higher velocity than ZF for oblique stimuli
outcomes.notes: Under reading (b), motion at 90 degrees or more, DC are significantly faster than ZF for right (p = 0.0002) and backward right (p = 0.0047), 2 of 4; under reading (a), the intercardinal directions, for 1 of 4 (backward right). Backward motion also differs (p = 0.0002).
deviations: The legend's "oblique" can be read two ways; the claim is reproduced under one of them (b) and not under the other (a).

outcomes.statement: Both species follow the direction of optic flow, turning right (positive angular velocity) to rightward motion and left to leftward motion.
outcomes.source: Figure 1G; Results, Optic flow induces angular matching and turns in DC, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Median angular velocity shows that both species follow the direction of optic flow, with positive and negative angular velocity indicating rightward and leftward turning, respectively
outcomes.notes: ZF turn with the motion; the rightward minus leftward difference is positive in 23 of 25 fish (median 29.51 deg/s, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 9.8e-07). DC do not by this test; 7 of 12 positive, median 0.88 deg/s, p = 0.151, and the DC median for left motion is +0.25 deg/s, the same sign as the paper's code printed (+0.3). DC turn right to right motion (8.67 deg/s).
deviations: The paper gives no test for following the direction; the per-fish rightward minus leftward difference and its test were chosen here before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: Across directional stimuli ZF have higher angular acceleration than DC, and the distributions of the two species differ for every stimulus.
outcomes.source: Results, Optic flow induces angular matching and turns in DC, paragraph 2; Figure 1H (Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni correction)
outcomes.quote: Across directional stimuli, ZF maintained higher angular acceleration than DC
outcomes.notes: With angular acceleration as the Methods define it, DC are higher than ZF for all nine stimuli (medians 143 to 191 against 55.4 to 66.4 deg/s2, Kruskal-Wallis p below 0.05/9 for each), the reverse of the claim. Per-fish medians, and the files at 128 to 171 Hz alone (ZF 84.9, DC 178.6 deg/s2, p = 6.3e-05), give the same. The quantity Fig1-S1.ipynb computes gives ZF higher with p below 0.05/9 for 7 of 9 stimuli; it divides the heading change per frame by the file's mean frame interval, which in DC files is a median 8.73 times the frame interval (ZF 1.37), as DC files hold only trial frames. Part of the DC values may be tracking noise. In the 3 s stationary phase the DC median is 205 deg/s2, higher than the 171 during motion (per fish median ratio 1.24, p = 0.016), but ZF are also higher at rest (66.9 and 60.8, ratio 1.07, p = 0.00012), so this does not separate the species. In frames where the fish is still (below 1 mm/s) DC are higher than ZF (per-fish medians 72.4 and 34.9 deg/s2, Mann-Whitney p = 0.00014), and DC are higher in every speed band (at 5 mm/s or more, 207 and 85.8). The outputs cannot say whether the higher values in moving DC are noise or turning during continuous swimming. With the heading from the unwrapped `f0_theta` DC are higher still (218 to 278 against ZF 61.8 to 77.3 deg/s2, 0 of 9). The reversal should not be read as evidence against the paper.
deviations: Follows the Methods' definition (degrees per second squared) on heading resampled to 30 Hz; the code's quantity, which disagrees with the Methods, is shown as a variant.
Heading is taken from the cumulative sum of `f0_vtheta`, as the code does; in DC files it does not match `f0_theta`.

outcomes.statement: DC generally respond less than ZF to monocular stimuli, suggesting that they need more visual motion input to drive the optomotor response.
outcomes.source: Results, Optic flow induces angular matching and turns in DC, paragraph 2; Figure S1E
outcomes.quote: DC generally responded less to monocular stimuli, suggesting that DC require more visual motion input to drive OMR behaviors
outcomes.notes: Species effect F = 23.3, p = 2.5e-06. DC turn less toward the stimulus than ZF for medial stimuli (3.26 against 13.48 deg/s, p = 0.0003) and binocular ones (2.87 against 21.87, p = 0.0002). For lateral stimuli DC are below ZF only nominally (-1.07 against -0.13 deg/s, p = 0.96); neither species turns toward lateral motion. With the protocol file's assignment of codes 9 and 11, the lateral medians change sign and DC are no longer below ZF there, which would make the claim partially reproduced. The DC turning to codes 9 and 11 leans toward the protocol file's assignment (see stimulus-code-link), so the lateral part is fragile.
deviations: Codes 9 and 11 are assigned as the figure code has them; the stimulus software's conversion has them the other way, and the data do not settle it.

outcomes.statement: ZF swim in discrete bouts separated by glides, while DC swim continuously at a relatively constant velocity.
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1; Figure 1C and Figure S1D
outcomes.quote: These visually evoked bouts in ZF consist of sharp velocity increases ... followed by interbout glides, resulting in characteristic periodic patterns. While DC also match the optic flow direction, they swim continuously, maintaining a relatively constant velocity
outcomes.notes: The median-to-mean ratio of instantaneous speed is 0.306 in ZF (25 fish, 0.244 to 0.580) and 0.908 in DC (12 fish, 11 above 0.74, one at 0.140), Mann-Whitney p = 5.4e-05. It holds in files at 128 to 171 Hz alone (0.298 against 0.898, p = 0.0028) and in forward trials alone.
deviations: The paper shows this with representative traces and a bout analysis whose bout files are not in the dandiset; the measure was chosen here before the analysis.

outcomes.statement: In representative trials ZF bouts reach a peak velocity of 44.7 mm/s with a median of 1.8 mm/s, DC swim at a median of 13.7 mm/s to forward motion; to oblique motion ZF show a median angular velocity of 12.0 degrees/s and median peak angular acceleration of 174 degrees/s2, and DC an average peak of 103 degrees/s2 to rightward motion.
outcomes.source: Results, Larval DC exhibit higher average swimming speeds, paragraph 1, and Results, Optic flow induces angular matching and turns in DC, paragraph 1; Figure 1C, 1E and 1F
outcomes.quote: sharp velocity increases (peak velocity = 44.7 mm/s, median velocity = 1.8 mm/s) ... (median velocity = 13.7 mm/s ... increased angular velocity (median = 12.0 °/s) and rapid, instantaneous angular acceleration (median peak = 174 °/s2 ... (average peak, rightward motion = 103 °/s2
outcomes.notes: The numbers come from single representative fish and trials. Fig1-S1.ipynb selects them by the index of a data folder and a trial number (for example DC folder 29, trial 79), and the dandiset gives no mapping from those folders to its subjects, nor the original file names.

outcomes.statement: Both species have spatially intermixed, direction-selective neurons enriched in the pretectum and anterior hindbrain, and share the major functional response types.
outcomes.source: Figure 2B to 2F
outcomes.quote: DC contain spatially intermixed, directionally tuned neurons with sustained responses to visual motion, enriched in the lateralized retinorecipient pretectum (Pt) and the anterior hindbrain (aHB) ... both share major functional response types
outcomes.notes: The two-photon imaging data are not in the dandiset, which holds only freely swimming tracking. The GitLab repository the paper names for "all behavioral and imaging data" holds notebooks only, and no other dandiset of this lab or paper was found on the archive.

outcomes.source: Figure 3E and 3F
outcomes.quote: DC performed significantly longer swims than ZF (DC = 0.75 s, ZF = 0.29 s

findings.statement: The dandiset holds only the freely swimming tracking of Figure 1 and Figure S1. The two-photon imaging and the head-fixed tail tracking behind Figures 2 to 4 are not in it, and the GitLab repository the paper names for all behavioural and imaging data holds analysis notebooks only. Nine of the paper's main findings cannot be tested.

The stimulus codes 0 to 20 have no names or description in the files or the dandiset metadata. They can be named only from the paper's analysis notebook and the protocol file of its stimulus software.

The paper's analysis notebook labels code 9 as lateral right and 11 as lateral left, while its conversion of the stimulus software's names gives the reverse (it carries a remap that swaps them). The data do not settle which is right; zebrafish barely turn to either, and Danionella turn more to the right for code 11, which fits the stimulus software's assignment only if the fish turn with lateral motion.

Subject ids 0 to 11 are each used for one zebrafish and one Danionella cerebrum, so subject_id does not identify an animal. The archive's summary counts 25 subjects and lists only Danio rerio; the files hold 37 fish of two species.

f0_vtheta is stated in radians/s but holds the heading change per frame in radians, and f0_vx and f0_vy are stated in pixels/s but are per frame. In most Danionella files the sum of f0_vtheta over a trial does not match the change of f0_theta (median ratios 0.09 to 0.89).

18 of 25 zebrafish files and 1 of 12 Danionella files are sampled at 32 to 35 Hz, where the Methods state tracking at more than 150 Hz. Their timestamp intervals are regular (28.8 to 30.8 ms) and their trials last the protocol's 35 s, so these are the acquisition rates. Some measures differ with frame rate, such as the zebrafish static speed (8.31 against 4.50 mm/s).

No spatial scale is given; positions are in pixels. They are consistent with the 10 pixels per mm in the paper's code, except one Danionella file (sub-5) whose positions reach 1490 pixels against about 1120 in the others.

Zebrafish and Danionella files were exported differently. Zebrafish files keep untracked frames and frames between trials; Danionella files hold only tracked trial frames and add a `dist` series. The paper's code filters Danionella frames on a `vel` column that is not in the files.

The paper's code computes the angular acceleration of Figure 1H as the heading change per frame divided by the file's mean frame interval, an angular velocity. In Danionella files the mean interval includes the gaps between trials (a median 8.73 times the frame interval), which scales their values down. With the Methods' definition Danionella have the higher angular acceleration.

Figure 1H and its legend state a Kruskal-Wallis test with Bonferroni correction; the code runs two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, and its loop selects the stimulus with a variable left from an earlier loop, so the nine tests compare the same stimulus.

The Results state that Danionella lack the direction-dependent speed modulation of zebrafish, but the Tukey test printed by Fig1-S1.ipynb for Figure 1D finds three Danionella pairs significant (static against backward left, backward right and forward left, adjusted p 0.024 to 0.040), as this attempt does.

The `dist` series of the Danionella files does not agree with the positions; over the first 35 s of a trial its sum is a median 1.11 times the path length of the smoothed positions, with a 5th to 95th percentile of 0.31 to 3.79. The paper's speed check uses it, though computing the check from positions passes the same trials.
The Figure 1D legend gives 26 zebrafish; the paper's code lists 25, its ANOVA degrees of freedom fit 25, and the dandiset holds 25.
The dandiset holds the 25 zebrafish and 12 Danionella the code keeps after exclusion (its comments give 28 and 40 recorded). The dandiset does not say that the excluded fish were left out or why.
